title: Given a target throughput like 1000 transactions per second at 100 milliseconds per request, how do you estimate the number of concurrent requests, the memory you need, and the right heap size and garbage-collection configuration?
shortTitle: Target Throughput Estimation — From TPS and Latency to Concurrency, Heap, and GC Config

s1_definition.profdef: Throughput estimation applies Little's Law, which states that the average number of concurrent requests in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system. For a target of 1000 transactions per second at 100 milliseconds each, concurrency is 1000 times 0.1, which is 100 requests in flight at once. You then size memory by multiplying that concurrency by the per-request memory footprint to get the transient working set, add the steady-state heap for caches and pools, and choose a maximum heap with headroom. Finally you select and tune a garbage collector so that pause times stay within the latency budget at the resulting allocation rate.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must serve 1000 customers every second, and each customer takes 100 milliseconds at a counter. Little's Law says that at any instant you will have 1000 times a tenth of a second, which is 100 customers standing at counters simultaneously, so you need 100 counters' worth of space and supplies. If each customer needs a certain amount of desk paper (per-request memory), then 100 concurrent customers need 100 times that paper on the desks at once, plus the branch's permanent filing cabinets (caches). You then make sure the cleaning crew (garbage collector) can tidy desks fast enough that no customer waits too long.
s1_definition.oneliner: Concurrency equals throughput times latency, memory equals concurrency times per-request footprint plus steady state, and the garbage collector must clear that allocation inside the latency budget.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Throughput estimation applies Little's Law, which states that the average number of concurrent requests in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each request spends in the system. For a target of 1000 transactions per second at 100 milliseconds each, concurrency is 1000 times 0.1, which is 100 requests in flight at once. You then size memory by multiplying that concurrency by the per-request memory footprint to get the transient working set, add the steady-state heap for caches and pools, and choose a maximum heap with headroom. Finally you select and tune a garbage collector so that pause times stay within the latency budget at the resulting allocation rate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must serve 1000 customers every second, and each customer takes 100 milliseconds at a counter. Little's Law says that at any instant you will have 1000 times a tenth of a second, which is 100 customers standing at counters simultaneously, so you need 100 counters' worth of space and supplies. If each customer needs a certain amount of desk paper (per-request memory), then 100 concurrent customers need 100 times that paper on the desks at once, plus the branch's permanent filing cabinets (caches). You then make sure the cleaning crew (garbage collector) can tidy desks fast enough that no customer waits too long.

**One line to remember:** Concurrency equals throughput times latency, memory equals concurrency times per-request footprint plus steady state, and the garbage collector must clear that allocation inside the latency budget.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with Little's Law, the foundation. It says `L = λ × W`, where L is the average number of requests in the system, λ is the throughput (requests per second), and W is the average time in the system (seconds). For 1000 TPS at 100 milliseconds, L = 1000 × 0.1 = 100. So on average 100 requests are being processed at any instant. This number drives everything: it tells you roughly how many worker threads you need (if the work is IO-bound you need at least about 100 threads so you are not the bottleneck) and how many request object graphs exist simultaneously.

Next, convert concurrency to memory. If you measured, as in the per-request overhead analysis, that one request retains about 2 megabytes at its peak (request object, domain graph, JSON buffers), then 100 concurrent requests have a transient working set of about 100 × 2 = 200 megabytes live at once. On top of that you add the steady-state heap: application caches, connection pools, loaded reference data, framework overhead — say another 300 megabytes. So the live set under load is roughly 500 megabytes.

```java
double tps = 1000;
double latencySeconds = 0.100;
double concurrency = tps * latencySeconds;            // Little's Law → 100
long perRequestBytes = 2L * 1024 * 1024;              // 2 MB measured
long transientSet = (long) concurrency * perRequestBytes;   // ~200 MB
long steadyState = 300L * 1024 * 1024;               // caches, pools
long liveSet = transientSet + steadyState;           // ~500 MB
```

Now size the heap. A common rule of thumb is to set the maximum heap to roughly two to three times the live set so the collector has room to work without constant full collections. With a 500-megabyte live set you might choose `-Xmx1500m` to `-Xmx2g`. You set the initial heap equal to the maximum (`-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`) on servers to avoid runtime resizing pauses. Too small a heap means frequent collections and high pause frequency; too large a heap wastes memory and can lengthen individual pauses with some collectors.

The allocation rate is the other critical number. If each request allocates, say, 4 megabytes including garbage (allocation is always higher than retained because of intermediate objects), then at 1000 TPS the allocation rate is about 4 gigabytes per second. The garbage collector must reclaim that fast enough. This is where collector choice matters.

```java
double allocPerRequestMB = 4;                         // measured allocation, not retained
double allocationRateGBps = (tps * allocPerRequestMB) / 1024;   // ~3.9 GB/s
```

For collector selection: G1GC (the default since Java 9) targets a pause-time goal you set with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`, which makes it a good general choice for a 100-millisecond latency budget. For very low and consistent pause requirements at larger heaps, ZGC or Shenandoah keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds by doing most work concurrently, at some throughput cost. The Parallel collector maximizes raw throughput but has longer stop-the-world pauses, so it suits batch jobs, not latency-sensitive APIs. The reasoning is always the same: match the collector's pause behavior to your latency budget and its throughput to your allocation rate.

```bash
# G1 tuned to the latency budget
-Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50 -XX:+ParallelRefProcEnabled
```

A senior nuance: these are capacity-planning estimates to size the first deployment, not final truth. You validate with a load test at the target 1000 TPS, watch P99 latency, GC pause time, and allocation rate, and adjust heap and collector flags from real data. You also plan headroom for bursts above the average and for the fact that latency and throughput are coupled — if latency rises under load, Little's Law says concurrency rises too, which increases memory and can spiral, so you protect the system with bounded pools and admission control.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is launching a payments API that must sustain 1000 transactions per second, where each transfer between accounts like Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 takes about 100 milliseconds. The capacity team must size the service before launch.

Problem 1 — How many requests at once? The team guessed and under-provisioned threads, so requests queued and latency ballooned. The fix is Little's Law: 1000 TPS times 0.1 seconds is 100 concurrent requests, so they need at least about 100 worker threads and must plan for 100 live request object graphs.

Problem 2 — How much heap? They picked a heap size at random and hit constant garbage collection. The fix is to multiply concurrency by the measured per-request footprint to get the transient set, add steady-state heap, and set the maximum heap to a few times the live set.

Problem 3 — Which collector and pauses? They used default settings and saw occasional 400-millisecond pauses that blew the latency budget. The fix is to compute the allocation rate from throughput and per-request allocation, then choose G1 with an explicit pause-time goal inside the latency budget.

The mini-project builds a `CapacityPlanner` that computes concurrency, transient memory, recommended heap, and allocation rate from the targets, and a demo plus tests that assert Little's Law gives 100 concurrency and that the recommended heap grows with per-request memory.

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a target of 1000 TPS, 100 milliseconds latency, 2 megabytes retained per request, and 4 megabytes allocated per request.

**Step 1.** The planner applies Little's Law: 1000 times 0.1 seconds equals 100 concurrent requests. This single number tells us we need at least about 100 worker threads and that 100 request object graphs are alive at once.

**Step 2.** The planner multiplies concurrency by the retained footprint: 100 times 2 megabytes equals a 200-megabyte transient working set — the memory live purely because of in-flight requests.

**Step 3.** It adds the steady-state heap for caches and pools, 300 megabytes, giving a 500-megabyte live set under load.

**Step 4.** It multiplies the live set by the heap multiplier of three to leave room for the collector, recommending about 1500 megabytes of maximum heap, which rounds up to a 2-gigabyte setting with headroom.

**Step 5.** It computes the allocation rate from throughput and per-request allocation: 1000 times 4 megabytes equals about 3.9 gigabytes per second of garbage the collector must reclaim.

**Step 6.** Given the 100-millisecond latency budget and that allocation rate, it recommends G1GC with a 50-millisecond pause-time goal, leaving half the budget for the request itself, and notes this must be validated with a real load test.

    │

    │

    │    heap = liveSet × 3 = 1500MB  →  -Xms2g -Xmx2g

  │  ──────────────────────────────────  │
  │  + concurrency(tps, latencyMs):      │  Little's Law: tps × latency
  │       double                         │
  │  + plan(tps, latency, retained,      │  full capacity calculation
  │       allocMB): CapacityPlan         │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                     │ builds
                     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CapacityPlan  (immutable)           │
  │  - concurrency: double               │
  │  - transientBytes: long              │
  │  - recommendedHeapBytes: long        │
  │  - allocationRateGBps: double        │
  │  + getters                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Method Contract: plan(tps, latencyMs, retained, allocMB) ──
    Pre:  tps > 0, latencyMs > 0
    Post: concurrency = tps × latencyMs/1000
          transient = concurrency × retained
          heap = (transient + steadyState) × 3
          allocRate = tps × allocMB / 1024
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException if tps<=0 or latencyMs<=0

  ── Sizing Decision Chain ───────────────────────────────
  1. concurrency = TPS × latency           (Little's Law)
  2. transient   = concurrency × per-req   (working set)
  3. liveSet     = transient + steadyState
  4. heap        = liveSet × 2–3           (-Xms = -Xmx)
  5. allocRate   = TPS × per-req-alloc     (GC pressure)
  6. GC          = G1 + MaxGCPauseMillis < budget; ZGC if stricter
  7. VALIDATE    = load test → adjust from real P99/pauses
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Capacity planning for a throughput target starts with Little's Law, which says the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the time each request spends in the system. For a target of one thousand transactions per second at one hundred milliseconds each, that is one thousand times a tenth of a second, which is one hundred concurrent requests. That single number drives everything downstream: it tells me I need at least about one hundred worker threads so the thread pool is not the bottleneck, and that one hundred request object graphs are alive in the heap at any instant.

From concurrency I size memory. I take the per-request footprint I measured earlier — say two megabytes retained at peak for the request object, the domain graph, and the JSON buffers — and multiply by the one hundred concurrent requests to get a two-hundred-megabyte transient working set. I add the steady-state heap for caches, connection pools, and reference data, perhaps another three hundred megabytes, giving a live set around five hundred megabytes. I then set the maximum heap to roughly two to three times the live set so the collector has room to work, which lands around one and a half to two gigabytes, and I set the initial heap equal to the maximum on servers to avoid runtime resizing pauses.

The other number I always compute is the allocation rate, because it drives garbage-collection pressure. Allocation is higher than retained memory because of all the intermediate objects, so if each request allocates about four megabytes, then at one thousand transactions per second the collector must reclaim roughly four gigabytes per second. With a hundred-millisecond latency budget I choose G1GC and set an explicit pause-time goal of around fifty milliseconds, leaving the rest of the budget for the actual work. If the requirement were stricter and consistent low pauses at a large heap, I would consider ZGC or Shenandoah, which keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds by working mostly concurrently, accepting a little throughput cost.

The nuance I always stress is that this is capacity planning to size the first deployment, not final truth. I validate it with a load test at the real target, watch P99 latency, GC pause time, and allocation rate, and adjust the heap and collector flags from actual data. I also leave headroom for bursts and remember that latency and throughput are coupled — if latency rises under load, Little's Law says concurrency rises too, which increases memory and can spiral, so I protect the system with bounded thread pools and admission control. At National Bank of India this exact method took our payments API launch from random guessing and constant garbage collection to a predictable, validated configuration that held one thousand transactions per second within budget.
